sources.title: Uchimura Kanzo (Q485247), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Kanzo Uchimura', English description 'Japanese writer (1861-1930)', Japanese description 日本のキリスト教思想家, instance of human, born 1861 (two dates, 23 and 26 March, on record), died 1930-03-28, citizen of Japan, Korean label 우치무라 간조. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'UCHIMURA Kanzo', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (English and Japanese pages read, short biography by library staff). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: thinker and practitioner of religion, son of a Takasaki domain samurai; after Sapporo Agricultural College and work for the Ministry of Agriculture and Commerce he studied in the United States; in 1891 left the First Higher Middle School after being accused of refusing to worship the emperor at the unveiling ceremony for the Imperial Rescript on Education; thereafter lived by writing; in 1900 founded 'Seisho no kenkyu' (Biblical Studies) and advocated Mukyokai (Non-church Christianity) not dependent on existing denominations; spoke out against the Russo-Japanese War; main works include 'Japan and the Japanese' (1894, later 'Representative Men of Japan') and 'How I Became a Christian' (1895). Short reference biography, neutral in tone.

Kyoto University Graduate School of Letters, Japanese Philosophy Section, 'Uchimura Kanzo' (page read in full, in Japanese: short biography, outline of his thought, texts and a reference bibliography). Scholarly department summary: baptised in 1878; at Amherst in 1886 had the conversion experience after which his actions rested consistently on evangelical faith; the 1891 'lese-majeste incident' at the First Higher Middle School and his resignation; writing from then on; from 1897 English-column editor of the Yorozu Choho newspaper and, with Kotoku Shusui and Sakai Toshihiko, publicly known as a social critic; involved in the campaign against the Ashio copper-mine pollution; opposition to the Russo-Japanese War and, in 1903, resignation from the paper together with Kotoku and Sakai; 1898 'Tokyo Independent' magazine, 1900 'Seisho no kenkyu' and 1901 'Mukyokai'; a lay Christian all his life; the second-coming movement from 1918; death on 28 March 1930 and the magazine's last issue, no. 357; the epitaph 'I for Japan; Japan for the World; The World for Christ; And All for God'.

Sapporo Independent Christian Church, 'Kyokai no rekishi' (History of the church; page read in Japanese). Church-history account, independent of Uchimura's own writings: Christian students of the Sapporo Agricultural College, among them Uchimura, Miyabe Kingo and Nitobe Inazo, were baptised into different denominations and asked why believers in one faith should be divided; a Methodist missionary at Hakodate lent 400 dollars for a first chapel; on 2 October 1881 they held a first service and issued a four-article declaration of independence (including that spreading the gospel in Japan without foreign help is a duty of the Japanese); they repaid the debt in full by 28 December 1882, which Uchimura recorded as joy beyond words; later Uchimura supported the church for thirty years, with six preaching tours, and his 1913 letter to Miyabe asks for a church that is independent, non-denominational, democratic and biblical. Church-authored, admiring of its founders.

Koike Naoshi, 'Kanzo Uchimura: A Summary of His Life and Faith', Bulletin of the Muroran Institute of Technology (repository copy, English; read in the biographical sections). DISCIPLE'S MEMOIR, EYEWITNESS BUT ADMIRING: the author studied with Uchimura and recalls him; recounts the Sapporo Independent Church and the repaid 400-dollar debt, the 610-species fish list of 1884, his work as a male nurse at the Pennsylvania Institution for the Feeble-Minded in 1885, the 1891 Imperial Rescript incident (dated 9 January, asserting that he alone did not bow, was called a traitor, had stones thrown at his house and was dismissed), his work for the Yorozu Choho newspaper from 1897, his 1903 opposition to the Russo-Japanese War, the 1,000-mark German royalty that came when he was out of work, his 'Two J's' statement and his sending students to a remote village at his own expense. Contains an overstatement ('nobody in all Japan spoke against war except Uchimura') that other sources contradict, so only specific episodes are used.

Christopher Andrew Born, 'Native Roots and Foreign Grafts: The Spiritual Quest of Uchimura Kanzo', doctoral dissertation, Washington University in St. Louis, 2017 (open-access PDF, 319 pages; biographical chapter and passages on the Rescript incident, the Yorozu Choho years and the Biblical Study magazine read). SCHOLARLY CRITICAL STUDY: says he simply nodded rather than make the required bow at the 1891 ceremony, that opponents made it public, that newspapers attacked him, that he fell gravely ill with pneumonia and allowed a letter of resignation to be written for him while his second wife, who nursed him, died weeks later; later he left an Osaka school that soon closed; at the Yorozu Choho he wrote political criticism and satire and bitterly criticised foreign and native opponents, including missionaries and former-domain statesmen; when the publisher backed the government's belligerent line before the Russo-Japanese War he resigned as an ardent pacifist; his Biblical Study magazine had 2,500 to 5,000 monthly circulation and was the base of Mukyokai; he withdrew from public life until 1917 and then turned to Second Coming lectures. Calls his tone at times arrogant.

Richard H. Drummond, 'Uchimura, Kanzo', in 'Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions', ed. Gerald H. Anderson (New York: Macmillan Reference USA, 1998), p. 687, reprinted by the Boston University School of Theology History of Missiology site (read in full). Reference biography by a historian of Japanese Christianity: 'independence rather than rejection' was his contribution; with 'customary independence' he delayed asking for baptism until 1878; after altercations with the Methodist missionary leader at Sapporo he and seven others formed an independent church that became the pattern for later non-church assemblies; after 1888 he resigned from each of several schools over disagreement on principle; the 1891 rescript affair 'effectually ended his educational career' (it also says he later changed his mind and sent a colleague to bow for him from a sickbed); by 1897 senior editor of the Yorozu Choho with outstanding success; from 1900 his magazine 'Seisho no Kenkyu' ran to 357 issues; he taught the Bible on Sundays at the request of Nitobe Inazo, then president of the First Higher School.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_uchimura_sapporo, src_uchimura_drummond, src_uchimura_born, src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_koike | 1878-1903 | church history, reference biography, scholarly dissertation, university summary, disciple's memoir] In 1881 he and fellow Sapporo students rejected division into denominations and issued a declaration of independence from foreign help (church history); with his 'customary independence' he delayed baptism and later split from the Methodist missionary leader (reference biography); he resigned from several schools over disagreements of principle; in 1903 he left the newspaper rather than follow its turn to war (dissertation, university summary); and he founded a non-denominational lay movement. Documented across five sources, though they largely retell the same few episodes. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The five sources retell a few shared episodes (the Sapporo church, the rescript ceremony and the 1903 resignation), and accounts of the 1891 episode conflict.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_uchimura_sapporo, src_uchimura_born, src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_koike | 1881-1930 | church history, scholarly dissertation, university summary, disciple's memoir] The Sapporo group declared that spreading the gospel without foreign help was the duty of the Japanese and repaid the missionary's loan, he stayed a lay Christian for life and built a movement with no denomination, buildings, sacraments or formal organisation, the magazine being its only centre (dissertation), and in 1926 he wrote that he could accept no faith that came in the name of foreigners (disciple's memoir). The need for independence is documented, but it overlaps heavily with the evidence for independent thinking. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The evidence overlaps almost entirely with the independent-thinking row and the 1926 statement is a disciple's quotation of his own words.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_uchimura_born, src_uchimura_koike, src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_drummond | 1891-1903 | scholarly dissertation, disciple's memoir, university summary, reference biography] After the 1891 rescript ceremony he was attacked in the press and by the public and lost his post (all four sources agree on the outcome); at the Yorozu Choho he bitterly criticised former-domain statesmen, Fukuzawa Yukichi and missionaries (dissertation); and in 1903 he resigned from the paper when it backed war (dissertation, university summary). Against this, accounts of the 1891 episode differ (a full refusal, a mere nod, a resignation letter written for him while ill, a later bow by proxy), so his firmness in that one moment is less clear than the pattern. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The accounts of the 1891 episode disagree (full refusal, nod, resignation letter written for him, bow by proxy), so the best-known instance is the least secure.

persistence.rationale: [src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_drummond, src_uchimura_born | 1900-1930 | university summary, reference biography, scholarly dissertation] He published the monthly 'Seisho no kenkyu' from September 1900 until his death in March 1930, 357 issues in all (university summary, reference biography), kept it going through the years after he left the newspaper and withdrew from public life (dissertation), and the circulation was 2,500 to 5,000 copies. The long run is documented; his effort behind it is inferred.

social_assertiveness.rationale: [src_uchimura_born, src_uchimura_koike, src_uchimura_drummond | 1897-1903 | scholarly dissertation, disciple's memoir, reference biography] For six years he wrote political criticism, satire and polemic in the Yorozu Choho and 'bitterly' criticised named opponents (dissertation); the disciple recalls a 'curt' style that earned him the nickname of a Japanese Carlyle, and the reference biography says he was an outstandingly successful senior editor. The public voice is clear; how he behaved in person is not described. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The strongest descriptions are a follower's recollection and a dissertation's summary of his writing, and they describe his printed voice, not his behaviour face to face.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_uchimura_sapporo, src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_koike | 1881-1927 | church history, university summary, disciple's memoir] He helped found and then repay the debt of an independent church in Sapporo in 1881-82, started his own magazines in 1898 and 1900 and the Mukyokai in 1901, and, according to the disciple, sent students to a remote village in Yamagata at his own expense to teach the Bible. The founding acts are documented by two independent sources; the village mission rests on one disciple's recollection. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): Of three sources one is a disciple's recollection and the founding acts are mostly known through the church's own telling.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_uchimura_kyoto, src_uchimura_koike, src_uchimura_born | 1884-1903 | university summary, disciple's memoir, scholarly dissertation] The university summary quotes the epitaph 'I for Japan; Japan for the World; The World for Christ; And All for God' and notes his part in the Ashio mine campaign and in opposing the war; the disciple says he chose fisheries science to help Japan and then turned to teaching the Bible as the deeper remedy, and describes his 1885 work as a male nurse; the dissertation says his readers valued his sincerity. The concern for the country is consistent across sources, but the stated reasons are his own words relayed by a follower. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): The motive is stated through his own epitaph and a disciple's retelling of his reasons.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_uchimura_drummond, src_uchimura_sapporo, src_uchimura_koike | 1881-1901 | reference biography, church history, disciple's memoir] The reference biography says his positive contribution was 'independence rather than rejection', a non-sacramental, largely non-liturgical form of church life; the Sapporo church credits his argument against baptism and communion rites for its own abolition of them in 1901; and the disciple calls Mukyokai something he originated. How new the idea was, set against earlier independent-church groups, is not examined in these sources. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): Novelty is asserted by a disciple and a reference work, and none of the sources compares his idea with earlier independent-church models.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_uchimura_born, src_uchimura_drummond, src_uchimura_kyoto | 1891-1918 | scholarly dissertation, reference biography, university summary] The dissertation reads his turn in 1917-18 from public pacifism and social comment to lectures on the Second Coming as a response to the failure of human efforts for peace, and the reference biography says that after the 1891 affair he later changed his mind about bowing; both readings are partly interpretive and the bow account is disputed by other sources. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): One instance is an interpretive reading by a single dissertation and the other is a contested account of the bow.

portrait.source: Studio portrait photograph of Uchimura Kanzo in his later years, photographer not named, printed as a plate with the printed caption 晩年の内村鑑三先生 ('Master Uchimura Kanzo in his late years') in the biography Uchimura Kanzo-den by Masumoto Shigeo and Fujisawa Otokichi (Tokyo: Uchimura Kanzo-den Kankokai, 1935; plate on page 5 of the digitised copy, National Diet Library Digital Collections item 1223422) and shown on the library's site 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures' as file 0240_2.jpg (835 x 1187 pixels). The shipped file is that image converted to RGB and downscaled to 703 x 1000, with no cropping and no upscaling. The library's record gives no photographer or photo date; the two authors are the book's authors, not named as photographers. The Wikimedia Commons copy of the same plate (Uchimura Kanzo.jpg, from page 5 of item 1223422) was compared by eye and shows the same pose.
portrait.license: Public domain: the National Diet Library states that all images in its 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures' exhibition are in the public domain and may be reused, including commercially, with source citation; the digital-collection item record (1223422) shows permission 'ooc' (the library's out-of-copyright class). Independent age basis: photograph of unknown authorship taken before the sitter's death in 1930 and published in Japan in 1935 at the latest, so protection under Japanese law (published before 1958) has expired and was not restored in the United States.
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown; plate in Uchimura Kanzo-den (Uchimura Kanzo-den Kankokai, 1935); source: National Diet Library, Japan, 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures' (https://www.ndl.go.jp/portrait/). Downscaled for display.
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer; reproduced in Uchimura Kanzo-den (authors Masumoto Shigeo and Fujisawa Otokichi)
portrait.date: before 1930 (undated; published as 'late years' in the 1935 biography)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: Stage B grade PLAUSIBLE (downgraded from strong because the item-level photographer/date was not holder-verified and the NDL item pages did not render); the lead (NDL Portraits record 240 with two photographs; Commons 'Uchimura Kanzo.jpg' 408x593 from Uchimura Kanzo-den) SURVIVED with a better file: instead of the Commons 408x593 crop, the NDL exhibit's own 835x1187 image 0240_2.jpg was downloaded from the NDL site. HOLDER FINDINGS: the exhibit page's source line is filled by a JavaScript data file that lists two photographs, digital-collection item 1170553 page 4 (Miyabe Kingo, Uchimura Kanzo-kun shoden, Dokuritsudo Shobo, 1932, caption 対米問題演説会当時の内村君, with a library stamp across the image) and item 1223422 page 5 (Masumoto Shigeo and Fujisawa Otokichi, Uchimura Kanzo-den, Uchimura Kanzo-den Kankokai, 1935); both item records read through the NDL item API show permission 'ooc' with no rights code (no iiif manifest, so the page scans could not be opened, not a bot wall as far as seen). 0240_2 (caption 晩年の内村鑑三先生) was matched to item 1223422 page 5 by comparing it with the Commons file taken from that page (same pose, different crop). The cleaner 1935 plate was chosen over the 1932 one with a stamp. NDL 'About this site' terms read (Japanese and the English parallel): all images public domain, reuse including commercial without application, cite source; NDL Terms of Use (Public Data License 1.0 default) read. Caveats: no photographer or date at the holder (Commons credits the book's authors as creators and dates 1925-05, neither confirmed, and neither is used); 'ooc' is read as the library's out-of-copyright class, and the legal basis is also the age path; the sitter is established by the printed caption naming him. Kind likeness. IDENTITY: QID verified live (2026-11-24) as Q485247, a human, born 1861 (two conflicting day values on record), died 1930-03-28, Korean label 우치무라 간조 (also the Korean Wikipedia title). Canonical name follows the lead's frozen list ('Uchimura Kanzō'). REGION east_asia, ERA 20th_century (his public career 1891-1930). Fields religion and literature are the nearest truthful ids. ATTRIBUTION: attributable for the scored episodes, which are dated and documented by several sources; but the 1891 rescript episode is reported in conflicting versions (no bow; a nod; a resignation letter written for him; a later bow by proxy), so the editorial text says accounts differ and no row relies on the firmness of that one moment. READ: NDL biography, Kyoto University page, Sapporo church history, Koike memoir (biographical sections), Born dissertation (biography and the passages on the rescript, Yorozu Choho and Biblical Study), Drummond entry. NOT OPENED IN FULL: Britannica, Howes 'Japan's Modern Prophet', Suzuki Norihisa's daily chronicle, the Hokkaido University Uchimura Library, Uchimura's own books. COUNTER-VOICES: Born's remark on his arrogance and bitterness, the disciple memoir's overstatement about antiwar loneliness (not used; Kotoku and Sakai resigned with him per the Kyoto page), the conflicting rescript accounts. Divorces, marriages and family deaths are not scored. Nine-row sparse profile (including no deep-focus, discipline or analytical rows).
